questions.stem: Which statement best describes an emergent property in a multicellular organism?

options.text: A whole-organism ability produced by interactions among integrated subsystems
options.why: An emergent property arises from organized interactions among parts. An effective whole-body response can’t be produced by one isolated component.

options.text: A specialized function that one cell performs without interacting with other cells
options.why: That describes cell specialization in isolation. Emergence depends on components interacting within a larger system.

options.text: A temporary change in an organ caused by damage to one of its tissues
options.why: That describes a possible effect of injury. Emergent properties are normal system-level abilities created by integration.

options.text: A structural level placed between an individual organ and the tissue forming it
options.why: Tissues form organs, and organs form body systems. An emergent property is an ability, not another structural level.

questions.stem: Which comparison between nervous and hormonal signaling is accurate?

options.text: Nervous signals are fast and targeted; hormones travel in blood and act more slowly
options.why: Neurons direct rapid signals toward connected effectors. Hormones circulate in blood and generally produce slower responses in cells with matching receptors.

options.text: Nervous signals travel in blood, whereas hormones pass directly along myelinated nerve fibres
options.why: The routes have been reversed. Hormones travel in blood, while nerve impulses travel along neurons.

options.text: Nervous signals always last for days, whereas every hormonal response ends within milliseconds
options.why: The timescales are backwards. Neural responses are usually brief, while hormonal effects commonly last longer.

options.text: Nervous signals affect every body cell, whereas hormones act only on the gland that secretes them
options.why: Neural output is directed to connected effectors. Hormones can travel widely but act on target cells with suitable receptors.

questions.stem: What would be visible in a transverse section of a typical mixed nerve?

options.text: One sensory neuron enclosed by a layer of skeletal muscle
options.why: A nerve contains many fibres rather than one neuron. Skeletal muscle can be an effector but doesn’t form the nerve sheath.

options.text: Myelinated and unmyelinated fibres in a protective sheath
options.why: A nerve is a protected bundle of nerve fibres. A mixed nerve contains fibres belonging to sensory and motor neurons.

options.text: Only motor neuron cell bodies surrounded by grey matter
options.why: Grey matter containing neuron cell bodies occurs in the central nervous system. A peripheral nerve section mainly shows bundled fibres.

options.text: A continuous tube carrying neurotransmitter between the brain and muscles
options.why: Neurotransmitters cross individual synapses; they don’t flow through a nerve tube. Electrical impulses travel along the fibres.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly traces a pain withdrawal reflex?

options.text: Pain receptor → motor neuron → interneuron → sensory neuron → skeletal muscle
options.why: Sensory input must reach the spinal cord before motor output leaves it. This option reverses the roles of sensory and motor neurons.

options.text: Pain receptor → sensory neuron → brain → endocrine gland → skeletal muscle
options.why: A spinal reflex doesn’t require an endocrine gland or prior integration by the brain. The spinal interneuron links sensory and motor stages.

options.text: Pain receptor → interneuron → sensory neuron → spinal cord → skeletal muscle
options.why: The receptor connects with a sensory neuron before the interneuron. Motor output is also missing between the spinal cord and muscle.

options.text: Pain receptor → sensory neuron → spinal interneuron → motor neuron → skeletal muscle
options.why: The sensory neuron brings input to the spinal cord, the interneuron processes it, and the motor neuron activates the skeletal muscle.

questions.stem: Which function belongs primarily to the cerebellum?

options.text: Detecting changes in blood carbon dioxide concentration
options.why: Chemoreceptors detect changes in blood chemistry. The cerebellum has a different role in movement.

options.text: Secreting melatonin during the hours of darkness
options.why: The pineal gland secretes melatonin. The cerebellum doesn’t produce the hormone that modulates sleep.

options.text: Coordinating muscle contractions and balance
options.why: The cerebellum coordinates the timing and force of muscular activity, helping movements remain smooth and balanced.

options.text: Integrating the interneuron pathway of a pain withdrawal reflex
options.why: The spinal cord integrates the pain withdrawal reflex. The cerebellum coordinates ongoing movement and balance.

questions.stem: Which pattern normally describes melatonin secretion and its effect?

options.text: It rises in daylight and directly causes skeletal muscle contraction
options.why: Melatonin normally falls during daylight, and it doesn’t act as a motor signal to skeletal muscle.

options.text: It rises in darkness and helps establish the daily sleep–wake cycle
options.why: The pineal gland normally secretes more melatonin during darkness. This daily pattern helps prepare the body for sleep.

options.text: It rises during exercise and increases blood glucose concentration
options.why: That describes part of the response to epinephrine. Melatonin is associated with circadian timing and sleep.

options.text: It falls in darkness and triggers conscious processing in the cerebral hemispheres
options.why: The secretion pattern is backwards. Melatonin modulates circadian sleep patterns rather than triggering conscious processing.

questions.stem: During vigorous exercise, which sequence produces an increase in ventilation rate?

options.text: More carbon dioxide → lower blood pH → chemoreceptor input → medulla → stronger respiratory muscle activity
options.why: Carbon dioxide-related pH change provides feedback to the brainstem. The medulla then increases signals to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles.

options.text: Higher blood pressure → pineal gland stimulation → melatonin release → faster diaphragm contraction
options.why: Melatonin regulates circadian sleep patterns and doesn’t relay cardiovascular feedback to respiratory muscles.

options.text: Less carbon dioxide → lower blood pH → baroreceptor input → reduced respiratory muscle activity
options.why: Less carbon dioxide would tend to raise blood pH. Baroreceptors monitor pressure rather than the chemical change described.

options.text: More oxygen → spinal pain receptor stimulation → motor output → slower intercostal muscle contraction
options.why: Pain receptors aren’t the sensors in ventilation feedback. Chemoreceptors monitor blood chemistry and signal the brainstem.

questions.stem: Which division of control correctly describes movement through the digestive system?

options.text: The enteric nervous system voluntarily initiates swallowing, while the cerebral hemispheres control all later contractions
options.why: The control assignments are reversed. Swallowing can be initiated voluntarily, while later peristalsis is controlled involuntarily by the enteric nervous system.

options.text: The central nervous system controls every contraction voluntarily from swallowing through egestion
options.why: Most movement through the gut occurs without voluntary control. The enteric nervous system coordinates the intervening peristaltic waves.

options.text: The central nervous system controls the voluntary endpoints, while the enteric nervous system controls intervening peristalsis
options.why: Initiation of swallowing and egestion can be voluntary. Between them, enteric circuits coordinate involuntary peristalsis.

options.text: The endocrine system contracts skeletal muscle throughout the gut, while nerves control only hormone release
options.why: Peristalsis involves gut-wall smooth muscle coordinated by the enteric nervous system. It isn’t a chain of skeletal muscle contractions.

questions.stem: A shoot receives light from one side and bends toward it. What directly causes the curvature?

options.text: Cells on the shaded side elongate more than cells on the illuminated side
options.why: An auxin gradient promotes greater elongation on the shaded side. Unequal growth makes the shoot curve toward the light.

options.text: Cells on the illuminated side divide rapidly while shaded cells stop growing
options.why: The expected mechanism depends on unequal cell elongation, not a contrast between rapid mitosis and complete growth arrest.

options.text: The whole shoot moves toward the light without changing its growth rate
options.why: Phototropism is directional growth, not locomotion of the whole plant. Different elongation rates produce the curve.

options.text: Auxin contracts cellulose fibres on the illuminated side of the shoot
options.why: Auxin promotes wall loosening and elongation on the shaded side. It doesn’t contract cellulose fibres.

questions.stem: How does auxin promote elongation of shoot cells?

options.text: It raises apoplast pH, strengthening cellulose cross-links so turgor pressure increases
options.why: The pH change is backwards, and stronger cross-links would resist expansion. Auxin promotes acidification and wall loosening.

options.text: It removes water from the cell, causing the cell wall to bend toward the vacuole
options.why: Water loss reduces turgor and doesn’t explain auxin-driven elongation. Expanding cells need a loosened wall acted on by internal pressure.

options.text: It stimulates lignin deposition, making the primary wall rigid enough to lengthen
options.why: Lignification makes walls more rigid and less able to elongate. Auxin acts through acidification and wall loosening.

options.text: It triggers H+ secretion into the apoplast, loosening cell-wall cross-links
options.why: Acidification loosens links within the wall, allowing it to extend as turgor pressure acts on the cell.

questions.stem: How can coordinated placement of auxin efflux carriers create an auxin gradient?

options.text: Carriers on one side of each cell direct auxin through the tissue
options.why: Asymmetric carrier placement gives auxin transport a consistent direction from cell to cell, allowing it to accumulate in one region.

options.text: Carriers destroy auxin on the illuminated side and synthesize it on the shaded side
options.why: Efflux carriers transport auxin out of cells; they neither destroy nor synthesize the hormone.

options.text: Carriers open pores that let all plant hormones diffuse equally in every direction
options.why: Equal movement in every direction wouldn’t maintain a gradient. The important feature is directional efflux caused by asymmetric placement.

options.text: Carriers bind light and pull auxin molecules mechanically toward the light source
options.why: Auxin efflux carriers are transport proteins, not light receptors or mechanical motors pulling molecules toward light.

questions.stem: Why is ethylene production during fruit ripening an example of positive feedback?

options.text: Ethylene slows ripening until the fruit’s internal conditions return to a set point
options.why: That would oppose the initial change and resemble negative feedback. Ethylene amplifies ripening instead.

options.text: Ethylene promotes ripening, and ripening stimulates further ethylene production
options.why: Each part of the loop strengthens the other, so the response accelerates and neighboring regions can ripen together.

options.text: Ethylene is consumed during ripening, causing its concentration to decrease continuously
options.why: A falling signal wouldn’t describe the amplifying loop. Ripening leads to increased ethylene production.

options.text: Ethylene transports cytokinin from roots and auxin from shoots at equal rates
options.why: That confuses two examples of plant integration. Ethylene regulates ripening rather than transporting auxin or cytokinin.
